searches.note: Thirty five searches of a share of forty five, ten left unspent, none of them the author's. Seventeen were restricted to a house's own domain (eyrievineyards.com four times, domainedrouhin.com and drouhin.com twice, domaineserene.com four times, argylewinery.com twice, cristomvineyards.com five times) and are read as primary through their summaries; three went to the appellation and wine bodies (the Oregon Wine Board, the Willamette Valley Wineries Association, TTB through the Federal Register and its archived press release); the rest kept the house's own domain out, and where the author had leant on them Wikipedia, Decanter, the Oregon Wine Press, the Drinks Business, Skurnik and The Prince of Pinot, so that each second source would be independent. Three searches served the whole group: the AVA dates, the Dundee Hills rule and Oregon's rule on grape names. No WebFetch was tried.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

The making, the blend and the sites went first to the house's own domain, read through its search summaries; the history went to the open web with the house's domain and the author's secondary sources kept out, so that each date found its second source elsewhere. The AVA dates went to TTB and the Oregon bodies.

Where a search contradicted the record it was set right with its source; where a detail was found in no source of this check it was cut or said with less. A distractor the explanation could only deny without a source was replaced, so that each question has one right answer that a source holds.

The dead are named with their dates where two sources agree (David Lett, 1939 to 2008, by the house's memorial biography and Decanter's obituary; Ken Evenstad, 1943 to 2020, by Drug Store News, the Star Tribune and the Oregon Wine Press); every living founder, heir and winemaker stays described.

The Prince of Pinot is a writer's own site and is cited neither in the fragment nor as a second source here; Argyle's citation of it gave way to the Oregon Wine Press. Wine with Seth, the Wine Economist and Wine Anorak, met among the results, are writers' own sites and are not cited. A magazine interview whose title names the founding winemaker of Cristom, who is living, is not cited either. The serving temperatures (13 to 15 for the pale South Block, 15 to 17 for Laurene and the Evenstad Reserve, 15 to 16 for the Mt. Jefferson, 9 to 11 for the long aged Brut) agree with the service reference; the house's own sheet gives 16 degrees for Laurene.

tested: The South Block's planting and its first bottling: the house's vineyard page and its sheets of 2017 and 2019 give ten rows planted in 1968 in a corner of the original vineyard where six soil types meet, first bottled on its own in 1975. Confirmed.
Own roots and no irrigation: the house's vineyard and grapegrowing pages say every vineyard is ungrafted and has never been irrigated or tilled. Confirmed.

The making: the house's winemaking page gives one new barrel in twenty five, native yeasts, minimal racking, long lees contact, a complete spontaneous malolactic, no fining and minimal filtration; its sheets give whole clusters at about five per cent at most and most fruit destemmed. Confirmed.
The founder's dates: 1939 to 2008 on the house's memorial biography; his death in 2008 in Decanter's obituary. Confirmed.

1965 and 1966: some three thousand cuttings set out in a nursery near Corvallis from February 1965 and a former prune orchard in the Dundee Hills found in 1966 (the house's pages, Polaner, the Oregon Wine History Archive). Cuttings, not young vines; retold.
The name: the hawks nesting in the firs above the first plantings (the house, Polaner, Visit McMinnville); one account credits the founder's wife, another the couple. Retold without the naming.
The respelling: EYE-ree in Visit McMinnville and Oregon Business. Added.
The first vintage of 1970: three accounts agree. Confirmed.

The tastings of 1979 and 1980: the Gault-Millau Olympiades of 330 wines from 33 countries and 62 judges, the 1975 among the leading Pinot Noirs (top ten, third or a win, by account); the rematch in Beaune, second by a fifth of a point to Drouhin's Chambolle-Musigny of 1959 (Decanter's Oregon's French connection, Wine Memories, Life in Vine). The story's ahead of several red Burgundies stands.

The hiatus: the founder's last South Block was 2007, and his son stopped the bottling in tribute (Leon and Son, the house's own page for the 2015), then revived it; 2013 or a gap of five or six years by account. Kept as revived.

The ageing: Decanter's account of the house's tasting of 2008 finds the 1970 alive and the 1975 the best of the early wines; the 1970 predates the separate South Block bottling. The named vintages are cut.

The label: Dundee Hills published in November 2004 and effective on 31 January 2005 (TTB's press release, the Federal Register); Oregon's 90 per cent for Pinot Noir, with eighteen varieties allowed the federal 75 (the Willamette Valley Wineries Association, the Oregon Wine Board). Retold.
The questions: one right answer each; the whole bunch distractor is false by the house's own five per cent. Sound.

The rules: nobody living named (the founder's wife and son described), no price (Decanter's release price and auction figures met and kept out), no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, British, no dash. Sound.

tested: Laurene: first made in 1992, named for the winemaker's eldest daughter, born that year, and called the house's flagship, all of the estate's own Pinot Noir in the Dundee Hills, chosen after the harvest from barrels with extra complexity, length and depth (the house's Our Wines page and its letters on Laurene). Confirmed; elder becomes eldest.

The making: hand picked into small boxes, destemmed, indigenous yeasts (the house's sheets of 2021 and 2023); fermentation of seven to twelve days with punching down and pumping over, twelve to fourteen months in French oak (the house's Learn More page); a fifth of the barrels new (the 2021 sheet). Confirmed.
The ageing and the serving: the house's sheet gives an optimum of ten to twelve years and a potential of fifteen, served at 16 degrees. Confirmed.

The dates: land bought in July 1987, the first wine of 1988 from bought fruit, the gravity winery of four levels built in 1989 (StarChefs, Advinetures, the house's Our Estate page, which also dates the building). Confirmed.
The soils: the house's pages say both its estates are of volcanic origin and name no series; Jory stands on the library and the region's summary; Nekia found nowhere. Retold.
The Gault-Millau tasting: many wines from many countries, not Pinot Noirs alone (three accounts, as for The Eyrie). Retold.
The questions: one right answer each; the story question's years are each in a source. Sound.

The rules: nobody living named (the head of the house, his daughter and her children described; the cuvees keep their names as wines'), no price, no score, nothing volatile (the estate's acreage met and kept out), no judging superlative, British, no dash. Sound.

tested: The founding in 1989, the hilltop site in the Dundee Hills, the first release, the 1990 Reserve, the Mark Bradford vineyard of 1993 named for the son, the building of 1913 in Carlton made a winery in 1994, the gravity winery of five levels finished in 2001 (the house's About page and timeline). Confirmed; the 1999 plans, the logging and the family name on the 1990 label were found nowhere.

The founder: born 9 July 1943, died 21 October 2020, aged 77; bought Upsher-Smith in 1968 or 1969 and ran it; founded the estate with his wife in 1989; a daughter named Serene and a son Mark (Drug Store News, the Star Tribune, the Beverage Journal). Confirmed.

The line from 1990 and the flagship: Great Northwest Wine traces the Evenstad Reserve to the inaugural vintage of 1990; Wine Enthusiast calls it the estate's flagship since 1990; Write for Wine gives the estate's name as the daughter's. Confirmed, without the family name on the first label.

The label and the oak: the house's sheets print Evenstad Reserve Pinot Noir, Willamette Valley; 15 to 17 months in French oak with 52 to 65 per cent new across 2015 to 2023. The record's well over a year and a good part new stand.

The glass: the house's own notes vary by vintage, from dark black cherry, sassafras, cola, lilac and bramble in a full body (2022) to rose and wild strawberry in a light body (2021). Retold to what recurs.

The estates and the Yamhill Cuvee: the house draws the Yamhill Cuvee from its estates in the Dundee Hills, the Eola-Amity Hills and Yamhill-Carlton, labelled Willamette Valley and named for Yamhill County; the Evenstad Reserve Chardonnay is labelled Dundee Hills. Confirmed; the sites line retold.
Chateau de la Cree in 2015: the Beverage Journal and the house's timeline. Confirmed.
The questions: one right answer each. Sound.

The rules: nobody living named (the founder's wife, daughter and son and every winemaker described; the vineyard keeps the son's given names as its own), no price (a release price and auction figures met and kept out), no score (a critic's points on the 1990 met and kept out), nothing volatile, no judging superlative, British, no dash. Sound.

tested: The founding in 1987, the hazelnut drying facility in Dundee called the Nuthouse, the first bottles riddled there, the Knudsen Vineyard as a source since 1987 and planted in 1971 or 1972, and the tirage library reaching back to the first vintage of 1987 (the house's brochures of 2017 and 2019, its Viticulture page and two of its history pages). Confirmed.

The Extended Tirage Brut: ten years on the yeast and disgorged on demand; base wines 75 to 90 per cent in stainless steel and the rest in neutral barrels; dosage of 2.5 to 4.5 grams a litre; Pinot Noir 55 to 60 per cent in 2010, 2011 and 2013 (the house's sheets). Confirmed; Meunier not found in those sheets.

The move to Newberg: winemaking relocated for the 2014 harvest to a former electronics plant in Newberg bought in 2013, the tasting room staying in Dundee in a Victorian farmhouse that had been the town hall, later a new Tasting House on the Dundee site (the Oregon Wine Press, Pamplin Media, Great Northwest Wine, the house's own history). Retold.
Brut and Champagne's minimum: the Codex's Champagne records give Brut under twelve grams and a vintage wine 36 months from tirage, of which twelve on the lees. Retold.
The questions: one right answer each; the explanation of the story question retold to the site rather than the building. Sound.

The rules: nobody living named (the founding winemakers and partners and the winemaker of 2013 described or left out), no price, no score, nothing volatile (the capacity of the Newberg plant met and kept out), no judging superlative, British, no dash; still in the story is still wine, not the present. Sound.

tested: The founding in 1992 and the name joined from the children's first names (the house's Our Story page, Dallas Wine Chick); one account gives 1991 for the purchase, the house 1992. Confirmed.

The Pellier winery: bonded in 1985 by members of the Mirassou family, on Spring Valley Road NW near Salem, and bought by the founders in 1992 (Oregon Wine History, Advinetures); the house names the Mirassou family as the planters of the first vineyard. Confirmed.

Marjorie: planted in 1982 to own rooted Pinot Noir by the earlier owners and renamed for the founder's mother, the one block kept while the rest was replanted from 1993 to 1996 (the house, Advinetures). Retold.
The bought grapes of 1992: found in no source; one account dates the first estate fruit to 1994. Cut.

The founding winemaker: at Calera from the harvest of 1978 for fourteen vintages, leaving in 1992 (Prince of Pinot read only as a pointer, an interview summary, Advinetures). Retold as the vintages of 1978 to 1991.

The Mt. Jefferson Cuvee: first vintage 1994 on the house's 2023 sheet and on a merchant's page; the house's flagship and the first of six Pinot Noirs released each year (Wine.com, Chambers Street); made from estate fruit alone for the first time in 2024 (the house's 2024 sheet). Confirmed.

The making: 43 to 52 per cent whole clusters, native yeasts, ten or eleven months on the lees, 16 to 26 per cent new French oak, unfined and unfiltered (the house's sheets of 2022 to 2024). Confirmed.
The sites: Columbia River basalt with Jory and Nekia among the series, the Van Duzer winds on the exposed blocks (the house's sheets for Royer and Eileen and its Vineyards page). Confirmed.

The label: the house's sheets print Willamette Valley as the appellation with Eola-Amity Hills as the sub-appellation; merchants print Eola-Amity Hills; no change of label was dated. The older vintages claim is cut.
The vineyards' names: Marjorie for the founder's mother, Jessie and Louise for his grandmothers, Eileen for his wife (the house). Each named for a woman of the family stands.
The questions: the Dujac distractor needed a denial no source gave; replaced. Sound.

The rules: nobody living named (the founders, their children and the founding winemaker described), no price (a release price met and kept out), no score (critics' points on the house's sheets kept out), nothing volatile (production met and kept out), no judging superlative, British, no dash. Sound.

Oregon's rule on grape names: 90 per cent for Pinot Noir and some fifty varieties, eighteen allowed the federal 75 (the Willamette Valley Wineries Association, the Oregon Wine Board).
